strengths: Clear problem formulation addressing the need for independent geometric control in anatomical structure generation without retraining
Comprehensive framework covering multiple aspects: size, shape, position control and multi-component compositional generation
Detailed implementation details provided in appendices with hyperparameter specifications and architectural choices
Multi-faceted evaluation approach including conditional fidelity, morphological metrics, pointcloud metrics, and biophysical simulations
Technically sound mathematical formulation using moment-based geometric constraints (mass, centroid, covariance)
Practical demonstration of applications including geometric inpainting and biophysical cardiac simulations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: primarily applies existing gradient-based guidance mechanisms to geometric constraints rather than proposing new methods

Weak baseline comparisons: most baselines are variations of the authors' own approach (explicit/implicit conditioning, cross-attention) with no comparison to state-of-the-art geometric control or anatomical generation methods from recent literature

Unclear improvements over baselines: Table 1 and Table 2 show minimal or inconsistent differences, and in some cases implicit conditioning performs similarly to geometric guidance, undermining the main contribution
Limited evaluation scope: restricted to cardiac segmentations from a single dataset (1204 images), with no evaluation on other anatomical structures or imaging modalities
Lack of statistical rigor: no significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple runs reported; no analysis of failure modes
Insufficient analysis of design choices: temperature parameter (10^-2), normalization constants (Table 6), and guidance weights lack justification or sensitivity analysis
Compositional generation marginal: Table 2 shows minimal improvement from multi-component control with some metrics degrading, undermining this key claimed contribution
Missing ethical and clinical considerations: no discussion of clinical validation, potential safety issues, or physiological realism beyond visual inspection

strengths: Novel and well-motivated framework using geometric moment losses to guide diffusion models without retraining, enabling interpretable and independent control over anatomical size, shape, and position
Solid mathematical formulation with three complementary conditioning approaches (explicit concatenation, implicit 3D Gaussian, cross-attention) that are thoughtfully designed and evaluated

Comprehensive experimental evaluation including morphological metrics (FD, Precision, Recall), point cloud metrics (MMD, COV, 1-NNA), ablation studies showing individual loss component contributions, and diverse qualitative demonstrations
Practical and clinically relevant applications demonstrated including disentangled generation, multi-component compositional control, and integration with biophysical simulations
Clear presentation with informative visualizations, well-structured paper, extensive implementation details and hyperparameters in appendices supporting reproducibility
weaknesses: Limited to single-dataset evaluation (TotalSegmentator, 596 cases) with no cross-dataset validation or external testing, raising significant generalization concerns and hindering claims about applicability to multiple anatomical structures

Insufficient baseline comparisons—mostly ablations of the proposed method rather than state-of-the-art external methods; missing comparisons with recent conditional generation approaches or other geometric control techniques

Quantitative improvements are often modest and sometimes marginal (e.g., Table 1 position loss: 34.9→28.4), with no statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or analysis of result robustness

Lack of rigorous quantitative evaluation of geometric constraint satisfaction—Figures 7-9 show qualitative evidence but no metrics for how precisely target geometric parameters are achieved or constraint violation rates
Missing computational analysis including inference time, memory requirements, scalability properties, and practical feasibility for clinical deployment

Limited theoretical justification for design choices—why L1 distance between geometric moments suffices, convergence properties, principled justification for loss weight factors (Table 5 appears empirically tuned)
Insufficient failure case analysis; Section 6 (Limitations) is brief and doesn't explore when/why the method breaks down, boundary conditions of applicability, or examples of problematic cases
No mention of code availability or release plans, limiting reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters provided

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear design requirements for anatomically controllable synthesis
Comprehensive multi-system experimental validation across cardiac, vascular, and skeletal structures
Practical demonstrations including biophysical simulation validation showing clinical relevance
Solid foundational approach using interpretable geometric moments for control
Detailed appendix with implementation details, datasets, and extensive ablation studies supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates compositional control of multiple anatomical substructures without retraining
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is a straightforward application of standard gradient-based guidance to geometric moments without new algorithmic or theoretical insights
Modest empirical improvements over baselines: Table 1 shows marginal differences in metrics, and baseline methods appear relatively simple and may not represent state-of-the-art
Evaluation heavily relies on controlled geometric metrics that directly measure loss objectives rather than independent validation of anatomical plausibility or realism
Insufficient justification for key design choices: geometric moment selection, weight factors (λ values appear ad-hoc), Mahalanobis distance choice lack principled justification and ablation

Incomplete and potentially unfair baseline comparison: unconditional+guidance vs conditional training not systematically compared; missing comparisons to recent conditional generation and other guidance approaches
Generalization concerns: primary cardiac dataset (596 cases) with manual filtering; unclear how method performs across populations and anatomical variants; limited cross-organ compositional control
Presentation issues: dense with many dispersed results making key insights unclear; important methodological details relegated to appendix
Simulation validation limited: single use case with simplified assumptions; no quantitative comparison to real patient outcomes or demonstration of superiority over alternatives
High hyperparameter sensitivity and manual tuning requirements (multiple weight factors, denoise steps) raise reproducibility concerns despite good appendix
Missing quantitative analysis of geometric disentanglement: attribute interference noted but not deeply investigated; claims of 'independent' control somewhat overstated

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem addressing genuine clinical need for realistic yet geometrically controllable anatomical generation
Technically sound mathematical framework with principled formulation of geometric guidance via differentiable moment losses
Exceptionally comprehensive experimental validation including multiple anatomies, diverse metrics, thorough ablations, and biophysical simulations
Demonstrated compositional and disentangled control of geometric attributes (size, shape, position independently)
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendix providing hyperparameters, implementation details, and methodology
Practical clinical demonstrations including geometric inpainting and multi-part control with complex non-convex geometries
Strong baseline comparisons across multiple conditioning paradigms with consistent advantages
Clear presentation with effective visualizations and accessible explanation of complex concepts
weaknesses: Limited core technical novelty—primarily combines standard diffusion models with straightforward moment computation; energy-based guidance builds directly on acknowledged prior work
Requires manual, dataset-specific weight tuning (λ₀, λ₁, λ₂) with no principled method provided; unclear how to select weights for new anatomies without extensive grid search
Moment-based geometric representation has fundamental limitations—cannot distinguish topologically distinct configurations with identical moments
Evaluation somewhat self-referential—fidelity metrics directly measure what the loss function optimizes; limited validation against real patient distributions
No computational cost analysis or runtime comparison with baselines; scalability to higher resolutions unclear
Incomplete baseline comparisons—conditional baselines appear to be authors' implementations; limited comparison with other recent anatomical editing methods
Minimal analysis of failure modes and when moment-based guidance breaks down; limited exploration of impossible or contradictory constraints
Narrow experimental scope—heavily weighted toward cardiac anatomy; generalization to other medical imaging domains and modalities unexplored
Missing sensitivity analyses for noise levels, latent initialization, and constraint interaction in compositional control
Code availability not mentioned; procedurally generated ellipsoid validation dataset somewhat artificial
